register: Colloquial Bangladeshi Bengali, romanized. tumi is the default level of address; apni is taught explicitly as the respectful one. The Bengali script is carried alongside every item so pronunciation reads real Bengali rather than an English approximation of it.
note: Original curriculum written for this app. Vocabulary reuses the v1 phrase id wherever the same item is taught, so spaced-repetition memory, the word bank and mistake history carry over.
legal_note: Not affiliated with, endorsed by, or derived from any commercial language course.

units.title: Your first words in Bengali
units.objective: Greet someone, thank them, and say yes and no.

examples.note: this one works at any time of day

question.prompt: Someone greets you with assalamualaikum. What do you say back?
question.explanation: A Bengali greeting is a matched pair: the reply is the same two words in the other order. Answering with assalamualaikum would be greeting them rather than replying to them.

units.title: How are you?
units.objective: Ask how someone is and say how you are.

question.prompt: You want to ask a friend how they are. Which is right?
question.explanation: The ending carries the person: -i belongs to ami, -o to tumi. Say achi about yourself and acho to whoever you are talking to.

units.title: Your name and mine
units.objective: Say your name, ask someone else's, and say you are learning Bengali.

question.prompt: tumi is "you". So how do you say "your name"?
question.explanation: Bengali changes the pronoun itself instead of adding a separate word: ami → amar, tumi → tomar, apni → apnar. The possessive comes first, just as it does in English.

units.title: This and that
units.objective: Point at things, name them, and say whose they are.

examples.note: achi is about a state, not a plain "is"

question.prompt: How do you say "that is my house"?
question.explanation: In the present tense Bengali simply leaves "is" out: the subject, then what it is. ach- is for being somewhere or being in a state, not for joining two nouns together.

question.prompt: You do have your book. Which is right?
question.explanation: Bengali has no verb "to have". It says the thing is (ache) or is not (nei) to you: amar boi ache is literally "my book is there".

question.prompt: How would you say "I want rice"?
question.explanation: Bengali puts the verb at the end of the sentence. Say who, then what, then the verb — and once you expect that, long sentences stop being confusing.

units.title: Hungry, thirsty, full
units.objective: Say how your body feels, and what you like.

examples.note: literally: hunger has come to me
but a mood stays with ami

question.prompt: How do you say "I am thirsty"?
question.explanation: Hunger and thirst are not things you are in Bengali — they are things that come over you. So they take amar, "to me", rather than ami.

lines.bengali: ami bhaat chai, ar ektu pani chai

questions.explanation: amar khide peyechhe — hunger has come over me.

units.title: Family and friends

notices.title: One word for he and she

examples.note: she covers he and she alike
and tar is his or her

question.prompt: You want to ask what your friend's sister is called. Which is right?
question.explanation: Bengali does not mark gender on its pronouns: she is he and she, and its possessive is tar for both. The change from she to tar is the same one you saw in ami → amar.

units.title: Asking questions

notices.title: Question words stay where they are

examples.note: ki sits where the name would go
kothay sits where the place would go
and koto where the price would go

question.prompt: "The shop is over there." To ask where it is, where does kothay go?
question.explanation: Bengali leaves the question word in the answer's own slot. Nothing moves to the front — the rise in your voice at the end does the rest.

units.title: What are you doing?

notices.title: Add -ch- and it is happening now

examples.note: plain: what I do in general
the person ending has not moved

question.prompt: kori is "I do". How do you say "I am doing"?
question.explanation: Slip -ch- in before the ending and the action becomes something happening at this moment. The ending itself does not change: kori → korchi, koro → korcho.

units.title: How you feel
units.objective: Say you are happy, tired or unwell.

notices.title: nei is the negative of achi

examples.note: and nei is how you say you have not got something

question.prompt: How do you say "I am not well"?
question.explanation: ach- is the one verb that does not take na. Its negative is a separate word, nei, and it replaces the verb entirely.

notices.title: Two ways to ask for the same thing

examples.note: to anyone you are showing respect to
-o again, so this is the friendly one

question.prompt: You are asking a shopkeeper you have never met to wait. Which do you say?
question.explanation: The -un ending is the respectful request; -o is for friends and family. Choosing the wrong one is the commonest way a polite sentence lands badly.

question.prompt: English says "to the shop". What does Bengali say?
question.explanation: Bengali puts the position word after the thing it positions — which is why they are called postpositions rather than prepositions. The rest of the sentence is unchanged.

units.title: Tea, thanks and goodbye
units.objective: Accept what you are offered and leave a home warmly.

phrase_patterns.english: could I have a little tea?

examples.english: could I have a little tea?
examples.note: literally: will a little tea happen?

question.prompt: You want to ask whether you may come in. Which is it?
question.explanation: Bengali makes a request by asking about what will happen rather than by adding a word for "please": ashbo? is "shall I come?", and the rising tone does the asking.

stories.title: Bondhur barite
stories.setup: Rachel visits her friend Nadia's family for the first time.

lines.english: A very beautiful house. May I sit?
Could I have a little tea?
I liked it a lot. Thank you.
I will go now. I will come again.

questions.prompt: What does Rachel ask for first?
questions.explanation: bhitore ashbo? — may I come in?
abar ashbo — I will come again.

dialogues.scenario: Tea in the front room, and then goodbye.

reply.english: yes, could I have a little tea?
no, thank you. I liked it a lot
I will come again. Everyone stay well

question.prompt: How would you say "today is cold"?
question.explanation: A weather sentence is just the day and the word for the weather. Bengali puts nothing between them — this is the same missing "is" you met with eta bhalo.

units.title: Care, and when it matters
units.objective: Say you care, reassure someone, and get help in a hurry.

notices.title: na after the verb makes it a "don't"

examples.note: the same na, after the same kind of verb

question.prompt: How do you tell a friend not to go?
question.explanation: Bengali negates by putting na after the verb, and the same rule turns a command into a "don't": jao (go) becomes jao na (don't go).

dialogues.scenario: A friend is unwell and you are getting help.

prompt.english: I am not well. My head hurts

reply.bengali: chinta koro na. amar daktar chai
reply.english: do not worry. I need a doctor
the hospital is to the right

prompt.english: thank you. you are a very good friend

dialogues.scenario: A whole afternoon in Bengali: arriving, tea, small talk, and home.

reply.english: yes, could I have a little tea?
I will come again. Everyone stay well
